plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000032) on the crossword's history (Wynne 1913, Simon & Schuster 1924, NYT 1942). Topic checked against all 31 ACT English passages. Every grammar choice set checked against the live bank with chsearch.py (an 'any other' comparison and a mid-sentence 'however' item were dropped because their sets matched items 208 and 198). Skills: date commas, register, neither/nor agreement, paragraph introduction, specific detail, decade apostrophe, irregular-plural possessive, imply/infer, 'Still' transition, sentence placement. Relabelled to the blind solvers' rating where it was lower: E032-04 medium→easy, E032-05 medium→easy, E032-07 medium→easy, E032-09 medium→easy, E032-10 hard→easy.

passages.title: Word-Cross
passages.text:
Most people who fill in a crossword never wonder who invented it. The answer is a British-born newspaper editor named Arthur Wynne. On December {{1|21 1913, the}} New York World printed his "Word-Cross" puzzle in its Sunday entertainment section. Wynne's grid was shaped like a diamond with an empty center, quite unlike the square grids of today's puzzles.

The puzzle caught on quickly, and readers {{2|went totally nuts for}} the new feature. Within a few weeks, a switch in the printed title had turned "Word-Cross" into "Cross-Word," and readers had begun mailing in puzzles of their own. Neither the paper's editors nor Wynne {{3|were}} prepared for how many arrived.

{{4|For about a decade, crosswords remained mostly a newspaper feature.}} Then, in 1924, two young publishers named Richard Simon and Max Schuster released a book of crossword puzzles with a pencil attached to each copy. The book {{5|did really well}}, and the success helped launch a publishing company that still exists. By the middle of the {{6|1920's}}, crosswords had become a national craze.

Not everyone was charmed. Some critics complained that the puzzles were wasting {{7|peoples'}} time, and the New York Times ran editorials that {{8|inferred}} solvers had nothing better to do.

[1] {{9|Still,}} the fad did not fade. [2] In 1942, the Times itself began publishing a crossword. [3] Its first puzzle editor, Margaret Farrar, set many of the rules that puzzle makers still follow. [4] Today, millions of people solve crosswords every day, in newspapers, in books, and on their phones. {{10|}}

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: In a month-day-year date inside a sentence, commas go after the day and after the year: "December 21, 1913, the New York World..."

A.rationale: A comma is needed between the day and the year.

C.rationale: When a full date appears mid-sentence, a comma must also follow the year.

D.rationale: A full date needs commas after the day and after the year.

hints: Where do commas go in a date like this?

strategy.explanation: Check both sides of the year.

candidates.remember: A full date in a sentence takes a comma after the day and after the year.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The essay is written in a straightforward informative style, so the clear, standard phrase "eagerly took up" fits; the others are slang.

A.rationale: "Went totally nuts for" is slang that does not match the essay's informative tone.

B.rationale: "Super into" is too casual for this essay.

D.rationale: "Big-time" is slang and too casual for this essay.

hints: Does the phrase sound like the rest of the essay?
candidates.remember: Choose wording that fits the essay's formal or informal level.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Neither the paper's editors nor Wynne
candidates.explanation: When subjects are joined by "neither ... nor," the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. "Wynne" is singular, so the verb is "was."

A.rationale: With "neither ... nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "Wynne," which is singular.

B.rationale: This is plural; the nearer subject, "Wynne," is singular.

C.rationale: This is plural and present tense; the essay describes a past event.

hints: Which subject is closer to the verb?

strategy.explanation: Find the subject nearest the verb.

candidates.remember: With either/or and neither/nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively introduces the paragraph?

choices.B: Arthur Wynne went on to edit puzzles for many more years.
choices.C: Newspapers in the early 1900s offered many kinds of entertainment.
choices.D: Many people today solve crosswords on their phones.

candidates.explanation: The next sentence begins "Then, in 1924," and describes the first crossword book. Saying that crosswords had remained mostly a newspaper feature sets up that change.

B.rationale: The paragraph is about the crossword's spread through a book, not about Wynne's later career.

C.rationale: This general statement does not set up the shift from newspapers to a book.

D.rationale: This jumps to the present and does not lead into "Then, in 1924."

hints: What does "Then" in the next sentence contrast with?
candidates.remember: A good opening sentence prepares for what the paragraph goes on to say.

candidates.stem: Which choice most specifically conveys how well the book sold?

choices.B: sold out its first printing and was reprinted again and again
choices.C: turned out to be a much bigger success than most books
choices.D: was very popular with a large number of readers everywhere

candidates.evidence: and the success helped launch a publishing company
candidates.explanation: Only B gives concrete evidence of strong sales: the first printing sold out and the book was reprinted repeatedly.

A.rationale: "Did really well" is vague and gives no specific information about sales.

C.rationale: This is still general; it does not say anything specific about sales.

D.rationale: "Very popular" and "a large number" are vague.

hints: Which choice gives something you could check?

strategy.explanation: Prefer concrete facts over general praise.

candidates.remember: "Specific" means concrete details, not stronger adjectives.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "The 1920s" simply names the ten years from 1920 to 1929; like other plurals that show no ownership, it takes no apostrophe.

A.rationale: A decade is a plural, not a possessive, so it takes no apostrophe before the s.

B.rationale: Nothing belongs to the decade, so no possessive apostrophe is needed.

D.rationale: This adds two apostrophes to a simple plural.

hints: Does the decade own anything here?

strategy.explanation: Ask whether the word shows ownership.

candidates.remember: Write decades as plurals without apostrophes: the 1920s.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Some critics complained that the puzzles were wasting
candidates.explanation: "People" is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so its possessive is formed by adding 's: "people's time."

A.rationale: "People" is already plural and does not end in s, so it takes 's, not s'.

B.rationale: The time belongs to the people, so a possessive apostrophe is needed.

C.rationale: This adds both an extra s and an apostrophe to a word that is already plural.

hints: Does "people" already mean more than one?

strategy.explanation: Form the plural first, then add the possessive.

candidates.remember: Plurals that don't end in s take 's: people's, children's.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: the New York Times ran editorials that
candidates.explanation: The editorials suggested something without stating it directly; a writer or speaker implies, while a reader or listener infers.

A.rationale: To infer is to draw a conclusion; the editorials suggested something, which is implying.

B.rationale: This is still the wrong word and also makes the sentence ungrammatical.

D.rationale: To impose is to force something on someone; it does not fit "that solvers had nothing better to do."

hints: Who is suggesting, and who is concluding?

strategy.explanation: Ask whether the subject is sending or receiving the idea.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The previous paragraph describes critics mocking crosswords; this sentence says the fad lasted anyway. "Still" signals that contrast.

B.rationale: "Indeed" would confirm the critics' view, but the sentence says the fad lasted in spite of it.

C.rationale: Nothing in the sentence is similar to the critics' complaints.

D.rationale: The fad did not last because of the criticism.

hints: Did the fad last because of the criticism or in spite of it?

strategy.explanation: Predict the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the paragraph:

The paper's editors reportedly believed that, in wartime, readers would welcome a distraction.

The sentence would most logically be placed after:
candidates.evidence: In 1942, the Times itself began publishing a crossword.
candidates.explanation: Sentence 2 says the Times began publishing a crossword in 1942, during World War II. The added sentence gives the editors' reason, so it belongs right after Sentence 2.

A.rationale: "The paper" would have no clear reference yet, and the Times has not begun its crossword.

C.rationale: The sentence explains why the Times began the crossword; placing it after Farrar's rules separates it from that event.

D.rationale: The sentence would interrupt the move to the present day and refer back to 1942 too late.

hints: Which sentence does the added sentence explain?

strategy.explanation: Find what "the paper" and "in wartime" refer to.

candidates.remember: An added sentence belongs right after the sentence it explains.
